scenes.title: Charging a Capacitor
scenes.topic: RC circuits — charging curve, time constant τ = RC

scenes.title: Moment of Inertia
scenes.topic: Moment of inertia — I = mr², quadratic radius scaling, disk integral I = ½MR²

scenes.title: Hoop vs Disk: Why a Disk Wins
scenes.topic: Rolling without slipping — energy conservation gives v = √(2gh / (1 + I/MR²)); disk beats hoop because less inertia goes into rotation

scenes.title: Hooke's Law: Why a Spring Bobs
scenes.topic: Simple harmonic motion of a spring — Hooke's law F = -kx leads to ω₀ = √(k/m) and period T = 2π√(m/k)

scenes.title: The Simple Pendulum: Why Mass Doesn't Matter
scenes.topic: Simple pendulum — for small swings, T = 2π√(L/g); the period depends on length and gravity, not mass

scenes.title: RLC and Pendulum: Same Math, Different Physics
scenes.topic: RLC ↔ pendulum analogy — both obey the same second-order linear ODE, with q↔x, I↔v, L↔m, 1/C↔k, R↔b

scenes.title: Centripetal Acceleration: Steering, Not Speeding
scenes.topic: Centripetal acceleration — uniform circular motion gives a = v²/r = rω², always pointing toward the centre

scenes.title: Steiner's Theorem: The Cost of an Off-Centre Axis
scenes.topic: Parallel-axis (Steiner's) theorem — I = I_cm + Md², the moment of inertia about any axis equals the inertia about a parallel axis through the centre of mass plus M times the squared offset

scenes.title: Damped Oscillation: Why Real Springs Stop
scenes.topic: Damped harmonic oscillator — adding velocity-proportional drag turns Hooke's law into m·ẍ + b·ẋ + k·x = 0; underdamped solution x(t) = A·e^(-γt)·sin(ωt+φ); regimes: underdamped, critically damped, overdamped

scenes.title: Torque: Why Leverage Beats Force
scenes.topic: Torque (Dreiemoment) — τ = rF sin θ; only the perpendicular component of a force creates rotation, peaking at θ = 90° and vanishing when force is parallel to the lever arm

scenes.title: Coulomb's Law: The Inverse-Square Tug
scenes.topic: Coulomb's law — F = k·q₁q₂/r²; force scales with the product of charges and the inverse square of distance; like repels, opposite attracts

scenes.title: Virtualizing the CPU: One Processor, Many Programs
scenes.topic: CPU virtualization — the OS gives each process the illusion of its own CPU by time-slicing one physical processor and performing context switches

scenes.title: fork(): One Process Becomes Two
scenes.topic: fork() duplicates the calling process — both parent and child return from the same call with different return values, and run concurrently from there

scenes.title: User Mode and Kernel Mode: The Trap Door
scenes.topic: User mode vs kernel mode — programs run directly on the CPU in user mode; a trap instruction is the only legal way to reach the kernel for privileged work, and a return-from-trap brings the CPU back

scenes.title: Round-Robin Scheduling: Fairness by the Slice
scenes.topic: Round-robin scheduling — give every ready job one fixed-length time slice in turn; short jobs respond fast, long jobs make steady progress

scenes.title: Address Translation: How a Page Table Finds the Bytes
scenes.topic: Paging address translation — a virtual address splits into VPN + offset; the VPN indexes a per-process page table to a physical frame number; the frame number plus the offset is the physical address

scenes.title: Race Condition: When Two Threads Share a Counter
scenes.topic: Race condition — two threads incrementing a shared counter can interleave their load-add-store steps so an increment is silently lost; fixing it needs a critical section

scenes.title: Test-and-Set: Building a Lock with One Atomic Instruction
scenes.topic: Test-and-set lock — a single atomic hardware instruction reads a flag's old value and writes one in the same step; threads that read zero own the lock, threads that read one spin until it is released

scenes.title: Address Space: Where Your Program Lives in Memory
scenes.topic: Address space layout — every process sees a virtual memory region with code at the bottom, static data above it, the heap growing up via malloc, and the stack growing down on each function call

scenes.title: The Inode: A File's Map to Its Blocks
scenes.topic: Inodes — every file has a fixed-size record holding its metadata and a list of pointers to the disk blocks that contain its bytes; direct pointers handle small files in one hop, indirect pointers fan out to reach large files via a tree of block pointers

scenes.title: Shortest Job First: Why Order Changes Wait Time
scenes.topic: Shortest Job First scheduling — three jobs arrive together; running them in arrival order versus shortest-first changes the average turnaround time even though the total work is identical

scenes.title: Producer–Consumer: When a Thread Needs to Wait
scenes.topic: Producer–consumer with condition variables — a bounded buffer fills and drains; a producer that finds the buffer full waits on a condition; a consumer that finds it empty waits on the other; signal wakes one waiter

scenes.title: TLB Hits and Misses: The Cost of a Page Table Lookup
scenes.topic: Translation Lookaside Buffer — a tiny on-chip cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations; a hit returns the frame number in a single cycle, a miss walks the page table and then fills the cache, dramatically slower

scenes.title: Semaphores: A Counter Threads Wait On
scenes.topic: Semaphores — a single integer plus a queue: P() decrements and blocks if the value would go negative, V() increments and wakes a waiter; a semaphore with initial value 1 acts as a lock

scenes.title: Process States: Running, Ready, Blocked
scenes.topic: Process states — a process is always in one of three states: RUNNING on the CPU, READY waiting for the CPU, or BLOCKED waiting on an I/O completion; the scheduler and I/O events drive every transition

scenes.title: Polling vs Interrupts: How the CPU Talks to a Slow Disk
scenes.topic: Polling vs interrupts — polling spins the CPU on a device status register until the device is ready; an interrupt lets the CPU run other work and be woken when the device is done. For a slow device the difference is most of the CPU's time.

scenes.title: Multi-Level Feedback Queue: A Scheduler That Learns
scenes.topic: MLFQ — three priority queues, jobs start at the top and get demoted when they use a whole time slice; a periodic priority boost lifts everyone back to the top to avoid starvation. Learns short vs long without knowing job lengths up front.

scenes.title: Dining Philosophers: A Deadlock by Symmetry
scenes.topic: Dining philosophers — five threads each need two shared chopsticks; if every philosopher grabs the left one first they all wait forever for the right. The four Coffman conditions for deadlock and how breaking symmetry breaks the cycle.

scenes.title: Demand Paging: When the Page Isn't in RAM
scenes.topic: Demand paging — virtual pages live on disk and are loaded into physical frames only when touched. The present bit, the page-fault trap, the swap-in animation, and what happens when RAM is full and a victim must be evicted first.

scenes.title: Journaling: Crash Consistency by Write-Ahead Log
scenes.topic: Crash consistency — a single file write touches data, inode, and bitmap; a crash partway through leaves the filesystem corrupt. A write-ahead journal records the intent first, then replays it on reboot so partial writes never become permanent.

scenes.title: RAID: Many Disks, One Logical Drive
scenes.topic: RAID — combining several disks to trade capacity for speed (striping, RAID-0), redundancy (mirroring, RAID-1), or both (parity, RAID-5). Visualises a block landing across multiple disks and what happens when one disk dies.

scenes.title: Voltage Divider: Why Two Resistors Split the Voltage
scenes.topic: Voltage divider — two resistors in series across a source put V_out = V_in · R2/(R1+R2) at the midpoint; sweeping R2 sweeps V_out proportionally

scenes.title: Half-Wave Rectifier: How a Diode Turns AC into Pulses
scenes.topic: Half-wave rectifier — a diode in series with a load conducts on positive half-cycles and blocks on negative, turning an AC sinusoid into a one-sided pulse train

scenes.title: D Flip-Flop: One Bit of Memory at the Clock Edge
scenes.topic: D flip-flop — an edge-triggered storage cell whose output Q samples the input D at every rising edge of the clock; the cell behind every register and counter

scenes.title: Kirchhoff's Voltage Law: Why a Loop Sums to Zero
scenes.topic: Kirchhoff's voltage law — walking around any closed loop, the sum of every voltage rise and drop equals zero; this is just energy conservation for charges returning to the same potential

scenes.title: Phasors: A Rotating Arrow Becomes a Sinusoid
scenes.topic: Phasor representation of an AC voltage — a vector of length V_m rotating at angular frequency ω; its real-axis projection traces v(t) = V_m cos(ωt + φ); two phasors at a fixed phase difference give two locked sinusoids

scenes.title: Karnaugh Maps: Grouping Adjacent Ones
scenes.topic: Karnaugh map minimization — a 3-variable function laid out on a Gray-coded grid; adjacent ones grouped into power-of-two rectangles collapse to the simplest sum-of-products form, beating algebra at its own game

scenes.title: Thévenin's Theorem: Any Linear Circuit Becomes One Source
scenes.topic: Thévenin's theorem — any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by an open-circuit voltage V_th in series with an equivalent resistance R_th; the load sees the same current and voltage either way

scenes.title: RC Low-Pass Filter: Why Gain Rolls Off at the Cutoff
scenes.topic: RC low-pass filter — transfer function H(jω) = 1/(1 + jωRC); gain stays flat below the cutoff ω_c = 1/RC and rolls off at −20 dB/decade above; Bode magnitude and phase together describe the filter at every frequency

scenes.title: Finite State Machines: A Circuit That Remembers Where It Was
scenes.topic: Finite state machines — a graph of states and labelled transitions models any sequential circuit; a Moore-style 11-detector with three states walks an input bit-stream and asserts its output whenever the last two bits were ones

scenes.title: Energy in a Capacitor: Why It's One Half C V Squared
scenes.topic: Energy stored in a capacitor — pushing charge against a rising voltage; the work integral ∫V dq from 0 to Q traces a triangle of area ½QV, giving the three equivalent forms ½CV², ½QV and Q²/(2C)

scenes.title: NAND is Universal: One Gate Builds Them All
scenes.topic: NAND universality — NOT, AND, and every Boolean function can be built from NAND gates alone; tying inputs together makes a NOT, chaining a NAND into a NOT makes an AND, signals propagate through the cascade with the truth table updating in real time

scenes.title: Inverting Op-Amp: The Virtual Short Does the Algebra
scenes.topic: Inverting op-amp — V+ grounded, V− driven to a virtual ground by feedback, KCL at the summing junction gives V_out = −(R_f/R_in)·V_in; the op-amp's own gain never enters the answer because the feedback loop forces V− to match V+

scenes.title: Euler's Method: Tangent Steps Along a Slope Field
scenes.topic: Euler's explicit method — march along a slope field by taking tangent steps. Small h hugs the true curve; large h drifts off step by step. Global error is first order in h.

scenes.title: Best Approximation: The Perpendicular Wins
scenes.topic: Best approximation theorem — the closest point in a subspace to a given vector is its orthogonal projection. A point u above a line L: dropping a perpendicular hits the foot uniquely, and any other candidate on the line is strictly farther by Pythagoras.

scenes.title: Gram-Schmidt: Subtract the Projection
scenes.topic: Gram-Schmidt orthogonalisation — keep v₁ as u₁; subtract the projection of v₂ onto u₁ so what's left (u₂) is perpendicular; normalise to get an orthonormal pair. The same recipe extends to 3D by subtracting both shadows in turn.

scenes.title: Change of Basis: P Converts the Reading
scenes.topic: Change-of-basis matrix — the same vector has different coordinate readings in two bases. Stack the new basis vectors as columns of P; then P times the new-basis coordinates returns the standard-basis coordinates of the same vector.

scenes.title: Rank, Nullity, and a Squashed Plane
scenes.topic: Rank-nullity by example — a singular 2×2 matrix squashes the whole plane down to one line. The image is that surviving line (rank 1); the kernel is the direction that collapsed onto the origin (nullity 1). Together they account for the dimension of the domain.

scenes.title: Dimension: How Many Free Directions?
scenes.topic: Dimension as a count of linearly independent directions — a single arrow gives a line (dim 1), a second non-collinear arrow sweeps out a plane (dim 2), and a third arrow off the plane fills three-dimensional space (dim 3).

scenes.title: Diagonalisation: Eigenvectors as Natural Axes
scenes.topic: A 2×2 matrix maps the unit circle to an ellipse. The two directions that stretch without rotating are the eigenvectors; their stretch factors are the eigenvalues. In the eigenbasis A is diagonal: A = PDP⁻¹.

scenes.title: Projection onto a Line
scenes.topic: Project a vector u onto the line spanned by v. The foot of the perpendicular is proj_v(u) — the closest point. The leftover u minus its projection is orthogonal to v. proj_v(u) = (u·v / v·v) v.

scenes.title: A Matrix Is a Function: T(v) = Av
scenes.topic: A matrix-vector multiplication is a linear transformation. Walk through input v, the matrix machine A, the row-by-column dot product, and the output Av. Every linear T from ℝⁿ to ℝⁿ is multiplication by a matrix.

scenes.title: Same Vector, Two Grids
scenes.topic: Change of basis — the same arrow has different coordinates depending on the grid it is measured against. Standard grid reads our vector as (1, 3); a tilted basis B = {b₁, b₂} reads the very same vector as (2, 1).

scenes.title: Span and Linear Dependence
scenes.topic: Span of two non-parallel 2D arrows is a parallelogram (the whole plane); a third arrow inside the span is linearly dependent; a third arrow off the plane lifts the span to all of ℝ³, demonstrating linear independence.

scenes.title: Linear Transformations: A Matrix Moves the Grid
scenes.topic: Linear transformation of the plane — every 2×2 matrix bends the standard grid in exactly one way, and its two columns are the images of the basis vectors e₁ and e₂. Rotation, scaling and shear are special cases of the same machine, closed off with a hero outro.

scenes.title: Euler vs RK4: Same Step Size, Different Curves
scenes.topic: Same ODE, same step size, two methods. Euler uses one tangent per step and drifts; classical Runge-Kutta samples four slopes per step, averages them, and hugs the true curve. A log-log error plot lays the order claim bare: slope 1 for Euler, slope 4 for RK4.

scenes.title: Second-Order ODE as a First-Order System
scenes.topic: A linear second-order ODE y'' + p y' + q y = 0 becomes a first-order system in two unknowns by introducing v = y'. The state vector (y, v) evolves under a single 2×2 matrix, opening up every first-order tool — Euler, RK4, eigenvector analysis.

scenes.title: Phase Portraits of a 2×2 Linear System
scenes.topic: For x' = A x with a 2×2 matrix A, the eigenvalues of A set the geometry of trajectories. Two negative real eigenvalues give a stable node; opposite signs give a saddle; a complex pair with negative real part gives a stable spiral.

scenes.title: Multivariable Limits Fail Along Different Paths
scenes.topic: A two-variable limit must agree along every path. For f(x, y) = (xy + y³)/(x² + y²), approaching the origin along the x-axis gives 0, while approaching along y = x gives 1/2. Two different values — so the limit does not exist.
concepts: limit of a function of two variables

scenes.title: Gradient and Level Curves: Perpendicular by Design
scenes.topic: On a contour plot, the gradient ∇f at every point is perpendicular to the level curve through that point. The gradient direction is steepest ascent; its length is the rate of steepest ascent. The directional derivative along the level-curve tangent is zero.

scenes.title: Directional Derivative: A Tilted Slice
scenes.topic: Directional derivative as the slope of a vertical slice. Pick a point on a surface z = f(x, y) and a unit direction u; the plane through that point parallel to u cuts the surface along a curve whose slope at the point is D_u f. Algebraically D_u f = ∇f · u, so every direction's slope is a projection of the gradient.

scenes.title: Linearisation: The Tangent Plane Snaps On
scenes.topic: Linear approximation of a surface near a point. Lead with the one-variable picture — a curve and its tangent line — then zoom in to feel that the error vanishes faster than the step. Generalises to L(x, y) = f(a, b) + f_x(a, b)(x − a) + f_y(a, b)(y − b), the equation of the tangent plane.

scenes.title: The Second-Derivative Test: A Discriminant Decides
scenes.topic: Classifying a critical point with the Hesse matrix. Three cases shown side by side: a bowl (D > 0, f_xx > 0) is a local minimum; a dome (D > 0, f_xx < 0) is a local maximum; a saddle (D < 0) is neither. The discriminant D = f_xx · f_yy − f_xy² and the sign of f_xx read the verdict off the matrix.

scenes.title: Hesse Eigenvalues: Curvature on the Principal Axes
scenes.topic: The Hesse matrix is symmetric, so it diagonalises in an orthonormal basis: its eigenvectors are the principal directions of curvature and its eigenvalues are the curvatures along them. Both eigenvalues positive — minimum; both negative — maximum; mixed signs — saddle. The discriminant just tracks the product λ₁ λ₂ = det H.

scenes.title: Global Extrema on a Triangle
scenes.topic: Finding the global min and max of f(x, y) = x² + y² − xy + x + y on the triangle x ≤ 0, y ≤ 0, x + y ≥ −3. Walks Plenum 6 problem 3 — the highest-leverage exam workout in chapter 6. Candidates: an interior critical point at (−1, −1), three edge minimisers, three corners. Min = −1 at the interior point; max = 6 at the two off-origin corners.

scenes.title: The MOSFET as a Switch: How a Voltage Opens a Channel
scenes.topic: NMOS as a digital switch — when V_GS is below the threshold V_t the channel is empty and the transistor is off; raise V_GS above V_t and a conducting channel forms, dropping R_DS and turning the transistor on. Wire it as an inverter and the output flips with the input.

scenes.title: BJT Load Line: Where the Operating Point Lives
scenes.topic: Common-emitter NPN amplifier — the DC load line V_CE = V_CC − I_C·R_C is fixed by the supply and the collector resistor; sweep the base current I_B and the operating point Q slides along that line through cutoff, the active region, and into saturation.

scenes.title: Two's Complement: How Computers Carry a Minus Sign
scenes.topic: Two's complement signed integers — flip every bit (one's complement) and add one to negate. The MSB becomes a sign bit, addition stays exactly the same as for unsigned integers, and a 4-bit register covers −8 to +7.

scenes.title: Kirchhoff's Current Law: Why a Node Adds to Zero
scenes.topic: Kirchhoff's current law — at every node, the sum of currents flowing in equals the sum of currents flowing out; this is charge conservation, since the node has no capacity to store charge

scenes.title: Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier: Both Halves of the Wave
scenes.topic: Full-wave bridge rectifier — four diodes arranged in a bridge route both halves of an AC sine wave through the load in the same direction; the output is the absolute value of the input, doubling the ripple frequency over a half-wave rectifier

scenes.title: 4-to-1 Multiplexer: Two Select Bits Pick a Wire
scenes.topic: 4-to-1 multiplexer — four data inputs (D0..D3) and two select inputs (S1, S0) feed into a logic block that routes whichever input is addressed by the select bits to a single output Y; demonstrates how 2^n select bits address 2^n data lines

scenes.title: Norton's Theorem: Any Linear Circuit Becomes One Current Source
scenes.topic: Norton's theorem — any linear two-terminal network can be replaced by a short-circuit current I_N in parallel with R_N = R_th; source transformation swaps freely between Thévenin and Norton forms

scenes.title: Non-Inverting Op-Amp: A Voltage Divider Sets the Gain
scenes.topic: Non-inverting op-amp configuration — V_in at V+, R1 ties V- to ground, R_f closes the loop from V_out to V-; virtual short forces V- = V_in, so V_out = (1 + R_f/R1)·V_in; gain is positive and always at least 1

scenes.title: Shift Register: A Bit Marches One Step per Clock Edge
scenes.topic: 4-bit serial-in / parallel-out shift register — four D flip-flops chained so each Q drives the next D, all sharing one clock; on every rising edge each cell samples its D pin, marching a bit pattern across the register one cell per clock pulse

scenes.title: Energy in an Inductor: Why It's One Half L I Squared
scenes.topic: Energy stored in an inductor — ramping current builds a magnetic field; the work integral ∫v·i dt collapses to ½LI² via Φ = L·I, giving the three equivalent forms ½LI², ½ΦI, and Φ²/(2L)

scenes.title: Maximum Power Transfer: Match the Load to the Source
scenes.topic: Maximum power transfer theorem — a source with internal resistance R_s delivers the most power into a load R_L when R_L equals R_s; the load power P_L = V_s²·R_L/(R_s+R_L)² peaks at R_L = R_s with value V_s²/(4R_s) and efficiency 50%

scenes.title: Joule Heating: How a Resistor Turns Current into Heat
scenes.topic: Joule heating in a resistor — every charge crossing a resistor drops potential V·q which becomes heat; instantaneous power P = V·I = I²R = V²/R; total dissipated energy W = P·t accumulates linearly while the current flows

scenes.title: Superposition: One Source at a Time
scenes.topic: Superposition: kill one source at a time, solve the linear sub-circuits, sum the responses.

scenes.title: Summing Amplifier: Add Voltages at the Virtual Ground
scenes.topic: Summing amplifier: KCL at the inverting node produces V_out = -R_f·Σ(V_k/R_k).

scenes.title: SR Latch: Two NOR Gates Remember a Bit
scenes.topic: Cross-coupled NOR gates form an SR latch — S sets Q=1, R resets Q=0, S=R=0 holds.

scenes.title: Ohm's Law: How Voltage, Current, and Resistance Connect
scenes.topic: Ohm's law — V = I·R; sweeping V scales I linearly, sweeping R bends I as 1/R.

scenes.title: Zener Clipper: A Diode That Caps the Peaks
scenes.topic: Zener diode reverse breakdown clamps a sine input's peaks to V_Z — clipper / regulator.

scenes.title: 2-to-4 Decoder: One-Hot Output Selection
scenes.topic: 2-to-4 decoder — two address bits drive four AND gates so exactly one output is high.

scenes.title: RC Charging: Why a Capacitor Fills on an Exponential Curve
scenes.topic: RC charging transient — a battery, resistor and capacitor in series; after the switch closes the capacitor voltage rises as V_C(t) = V_0(1 − e^{−t/τ}); the time constant τ = RC sets the speed (63% at one τ, ≈99% after five τ).

scenes.title: The CMOS Inverter: Two Transistors, Zero Static Power
scenes.topic: CMOS inverter — PMOS to V_DD, NMOS to ground, gates tied to V_in, drains tied to V_out. Only one transistor conducts at a time, so the output flips between V_DD and 0 with essentially no static current. Sweeping V_in across the threshold produces the sharp transfer curve at the heart of every digital logic family.

scenes.title: Counting in Hexadecimal: Four Bits, One Symbol
scenes.topic: Hexadecimal as a packing of binary — every 4-bit nibble maps to exactly one hex symbol 0..F; an 8-bit byte becomes two hex digits. The radix is base 16 with place values 16⁰, 16¹, 16², which is why programmers prefer hex for memory addresses, byte patterns, and machine code.

scenes.title: RL Transient: Why an Inductor Slows the Current
scenes.topic: Series RL transient — when the switch closes, current rises along i(t) = (V/R)(1 − e^{−t/τ}) with τ = L/R, because the inductor opposes any change in current and develops a back-emf that decays as the current settles; the inductive twin of RC charging.

scenes.title: The Integrator Op-Amp: Square Wave In, Triangle Wave Out
scenes.topic: Op-amp integrator — replace the inverting amp's feedback resistor with a capacitor and the virtual short turns the circuit into a time integrator V_out(t) = −(1/RC)∫V_in dt; a square-wave input produces a linear triangle-wave output whose slope is set by 1/RC.

scenes.title: JK Flip-Flop: The SR Latch With a Useful Fourth Row
scenes.topic: JK flip-flop — the SR latch with the forbidden S=R=1 state replaced by a TOGGLE mode (Q flips on each rising clock edge when J=K=1); the four modes hold/reset/set/toggle and the divide-by-two behaviour are the workhorse of every binary counter.

scenes.title: Source Transformations: A Battery and a Current Source Are the Same Thing
scenes.topic: Two-terminal equivalence between a voltage source in series with R and a current source in parallel with R — the live morph of a Thévenin network into its Norton counterpart, with open-circuit and short-circuit tests as the proof.

scenes.title: RLC Resonance: Where the Reactances Cancel
scenes.topic: Series RLC resonance — sweep frequency and watch the loop current peak at ω₀ = 1/√(LC) where X_L and X_C exactly cancel; three phasor diagrams show how V_L and V_C oppose perfectly at resonance, leaving only V_R.

scenes.title: Binary Addition: How the Carry Walks Left
scenes.topic: 4-bit binary addition column-by-column with the carry walking right-to-left — visualises 0101 + 0111 = 1100 (5 + 7 = 12) one column at a time, then motivates ripple-carry's worst-case delay in hardware.

scenes.title: Diode I-V Curve: How Current Climbs Past the Knee
scenes.topic: Silicon diode I-V characteristic — flat below ~0.6 V knee, exponentially climbing above; a triangular V_D sweep drives a marker Q along the curve while a live mono readout updates V_D and I_D in lockstep.

scenes.title: BJT Current Mirror: How Q2 Copies Q1's Current
scenes.topic: Two matched NPN transistors share a base-emitter voltage — Q1 is diode-connected with R_ref above, Q2 mirrors Q1's collector current into a load. A sweep of I_ref drives twin bar gauges that rise and fall in lockstep, demonstrating I_out = I_ref.

scenes.title: Full Adder: Three Bits In, Two Bits Out
scenes.topic: A full adder takes A, B, and a carry-in and produces a sum bit and a carry-out via two XORs, two ANDs and one OR. The walk-beat cycles all eight input combinations, with wires glowing amber when carrying a 1 and the active truth-table row highlighting.

scenes.title: Current Divider: How Two Parallel Resistors Split the Current
scenes.topic: Current divider — two resistors in parallel across a current source I_in split the total current as I_1 = I_in · R_2/(R_1+R_2) and I_2 = I_in · R_1/(R_1+R_2); the smaller resistor steals the larger share. Genuine animation in Beat 4: R_2 scrubs and the two branch-current arrows swell/shrink with live percentages.

scenes.title: RC High-Pass Filter: Why Gain Rolls In Past the Cutoff
scenes.topic: RC high-pass filter — capacitor in series, resistor to ground, V_out across the resistor; H(jω) = jωRC / (1 + jωRC); gain rises at +20 dB/decade below ω_c = 1/RC and is flat at 0 dB above; phase shifts from +90° (lead) down to 0°. Sister scene to low-pass-bode with the roles swapped.

scenes.title: Ripple Counter: How Four Toggle Flip-Flops Count to Sixteen
scenes.topic: 4-bit asynchronous ripple counter — chain four toggle (J = K = 1) flip-flops with each Q driving the next stage's clock. Each stage halves the frequency, so Q_0 is the LSB toggling every clock and Q_3 is the MSB toggling every eight clocks; together they spell out a binary count from 0 to 15. The 'ripple' name comes from the propagation-delay cascade — bits flip one stage at a time.

scenes.title: The Wheatstone Bridge: A Galvanometer That Lies Still at Balance
scenes.topic: Wheatstone bridge — four resistors in a diamond with a galvanometer between the two midpoints; the two midpoints reach the same voltage when R1·Rx = R2·R3, and the meter falls dead still. Genuine motion in Beat 4: Rx scrubs in real time and the galvanometer needle deflects, crossing zero at the balance point.

scenes.title: The Op-Amp Comparator: A Switch That Snaps at the Reference
scenes.topic: Open-loop op-amp as a comparator — strip away the feedback resistor and the enormous open-loop gain forces V_out to one of the supply rails the moment V_in crosses V_ref. Genuine motion in Beat 4: a triangle input sweeps through V_ref and the output snaps cleanly between +V_sat and −V_sat with synchronised scope traces.

scenes.title: 1-to-4 Demultiplexer: One Data Bit, Four Possible Outputs
scenes.topic: 1-to-4 demultiplexer — one data input D, two select bits S1 and S0, and four outputs Y0..Y3; the addressed output takes D, the others sit at zero. Genuine motion in Beat 4: the select address cycles 00→01→10→11, the active output line glows and a dot rides through the addressed AND gate while the inactive lines stay grey at 0.

scenes.title: The Diode Clamper: Lift the AC, Keep the Shape
scenes.topic: Positive diode clamper — a series capacitor and a shunt diode shift an AC sine wave upward by its peak so the negative peaks sit at zero, without changing the shape. The capacitor charges once on the first negative half-cycle and then acts as a constant DC offset on every cycle thereafter. Genuine motion in Beat 3: diode highlights, charge dots flow, V_C climbs to V_p, live readout panel. Genuine motion in Beat 4: synchronised scope traces of V_in (centred on zero) and V_out (centred on +V_p) with cursor + offset arrow.

scenes.title: The Power Triangle: Why Not Every Volt-Amp Becomes a Watt
scenes.topic: AC power decomposes into real power P (watts) along the in-phase axis, reactive power Q (vars) along the quadrature axis, and apparent power S (VA) as the hypotenuse. Sweeping the phase angle phi from 0 to 90 degrees morphs the triangle: P shrinks, Q grows, |S| stays fixed, cos phi (the power factor) falls from one to zero. Genuine motion in Beat 4: phi sweeps as a triangle wave, the triangle redraws each frame, live readout of P/S, Q/S, and cos phi.

scenes.title: The 8-to-3 Priority Encoder: When Many Speak, One Wins
scenes.topic: 8-to-3 priority encoder — eight input lines I0..I7, three output bits Y2 Y1 Y0, plus a Valid flag. The output is the 3-bit binary index of the highest-indexed active input; when multiple inputs are HIGH at once, the highest index wins and the others are ignored. Genuine motion in Beat 4: a sequence of curated input patterns plays out, with each frame computing the output bits and Valid flag from the current pattern in real time, and a halo highlighting the winning input.

scenes.title: Subspaces: Why the Origin Matters
scenes.topic: A subspace must contain the zero vector, be closed under addition, and be closed under scalar multiplication. A line through the origin passes all three tests. A line that misses the origin fails closure under addition — the parallelogram-rule sum of two of its vectors lands off the line, and the origin is not on the line either.

scenes.title: Linear Combinations: Mix Two Arrows
scenes.topic: A linear combination is the recipe a·v₁ + b·v₂ with two scalar dials. Fix b at zero and sweep a — the output point glides along a line through the origin. Sweep both dials at once and the output paints out a region of the plane. Two non-parallel arrows span all of ℝ².

scenes.title: The Determinant as Area
scenes.topic: A 2×2 matrix maps the unit square to a parallelogram whose signed area is det A = ad − bc. A continuous morph from identity to A shows the deformation; scrubbing one entry through det = 0 collapses the parallelogram to a line, then flips orientation as det goes negative.

scenes.title: The Emitter Follower: Gain of One, Current to Spare
scenes.topic: BJT common-collector amplifier — output sits one V_BE below the input, so voltage gain is about one, but the transistor delivers β times the input current. The canonical low-impedance buffer used at the end of audio output stages, op-amp followers, and line drivers.

scenes.title: The Schmitt Trigger: Why a Comparator Needs Hysteresis
scenes.topic: Inverting op-amp with positive feedback through R1/R2 creates two thresholds V_TH and V_TL — once the output snaps, the trigger ignores small input wiggles inside the band. The cure for chattering comparators that has to deal with noisy crossings.

scenes.title: T Flip-Flop: One Input, One Toggle per Edge
scenes.topic: Toggle flip-flop — when T=1, Q inverts on every rising clock edge; when T=0, Q holds. The frequency-divide-by-two building block of every binary counter and clock prescaler.

scenes.title: MOSFET Transfer Characteristic: A Quadratic Turns On at Threshold
scenes.topic: N-channel MOSFET transfer characteristic — below V_th the channel is off and I_D = 0; above V_th the saturation drain current grows as I_D = (k/2)(V_GS − V_th)². Sweep V_GS and watch the operating point trace the I_D vs V_GS curve from cutoff into saturation.

scenes.title: Voltage Doubler: Two Diodes Pump V Twice
scenes.topic: Half-wave Greinacher voltage doubler — on the negative half-cycle D1 conducts and C1 charges to V_p; on the positive half-cycle the source and C1 sit in series at 2V_p, D2 turns on, and C2 charges toward 2V_p. Cascading the same pair gives the Cockcroft–Walton multiplier.

scenes.title: Impedance Triangle: R + jX as One Phasor
scenes.topic: AC impedance for a series R-L-C — resistors carry pure R, inductors give +jωL, capacitors give −j/(ωC). Stack them on the complex plane and the net impedance Z = R + jX is one phasor with magnitude √(R² + X²) and angle arctan(X/R). Sweep ω and Z rotates from capacitive (below the axis) through resonance (on the axis) to inductive (above).

scenes.title: The Dot Product: Length, Length, Cosine
scenes.topic: Geometric meaning of the dot product — u·v equals ‖u‖ ‖v‖ cos θ. Hold one arrow fixed and spin the other; the dot-product readout sweeps in sync with the cosine. The sign alone reads off acute, right, or obtuse.

scenes.title: Orthogonal Complement: The Other Direction
scenes.topic: The orthogonal complement of a line W is the perpendicular line W⊥ through the origin. Every vector u splits uniquely as u = w + w⊥. Rotate u and the two pieces glide along their lines. Together W and W⊥ span the whole plane — the direct sum.

scenes.title: Least Squares: Project, Don't Solve
scenes.topic: Three noisy points, no line through all three. Tilt the slope and the sum of squared residuals rises and falls; the minimum sits where the error vector is perpendicular to the column space of A. That perpendicularity condition is the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb.

scenes.title: Lagrange Multipliers: When Gradients Align
scenes.topic: Constrained extrema by Lagrange multipliers — at a maximum or minimum of f along a constraint g(x, y) = c, the gradient of f is parallel to the gradient of g. Sliding a point along x² + y² = 2 with f = x + y, ∇f stays fixed pointing northeast while ∇g rotates with the point; the two arrows lock parallel at (1, 1) (max) and antiparallel at (−1, −1) (min). ∇f = λ∇g picks out the candidates.

scenes.title: Chain Rule on a Path: Gradient · Velocity
scenes.topic: Multivariable chain rule visualised. A particle moves along a parametric curve γ(t) on a contour map of f. As it crosses level curves the altitude z = f(γ(t)) rises and falls; the instantaneous rate dz/dt equals the gradient of f dotted with the velocity γ'(t). Concrete example: f(x, y) = x² + y², γ(t) = (cos t + 1, sin t). The particle traces a unit circle offset right; the live dot product ∇f · γ' tracks against the analytic value −2 sin t.

scenes.title: Critical Points: Where ∇f Vanishes
scenes.topic: Finding interior critical points by setting the gradient to zero. For f(x, y) = x³/3 − x + y² − 2y, plot the contour map plus the gradient vector field; sweep a scanner along y = 1 and watch |∇f| dip to zero at exactly x = −1 and x = +1. Solving the system ∇f = (x² − 1, 2y − 2) = (0, 0) recovers the same pair. Classification waits for the Hesse test.

scenes.title: Coordinates in a Basis Are Unique
scenes.topic: Given a basis {b₁, b₂} for the plane, every vector v has exactly one coordinate pair (a, b) with v = a·b₁ + b·b₂. Sweeping trial (a, b) values shows almost every guess misses; only one pair lands the trial point on v. Switch to a different basis {c₁, c₂} and the same v gets a new but again unique coordinate pair — the basis is the language, the coordinates are the word.

scenes.title: The Null Space Is a Line Through the Origin
scenes.topic: For the singular matrix M = [[1, 2], [2, 4]] the rows are multiples of each other, so M is not invertible. Sweeping a vector x along the direction d = (2, −1) shows M·x stays glued at the origin — every point on that line is in the null space. Stepping x off the line makes M·x jump along the image line y = 2x. The null space {x : M·x = 0} forms a one-dimensional subspace.

scenes.title: Polynomials Are Vectors Too
scenes.topic: A polynomial p(x) = a + b·x + c·x² is built from three numbers — its coordinates in the basis {1, x, x²}. Scrubbing the (a, b, c) triple morphs the coordinate vector and the polynomial graph in sync. Adding two polynomials adds their coordinate triples component-by-component. The space P₂ of polynomials of degree at most two is a three-dimensional vector space, with vectors that are not arrows at all.

scenes.title: Separable Variables: The Circle Family
scenes.topic: Separable first-order ODE technique — for dy/dx = -x/y, move all y's to one side and all x's to the other, integrate each side, and the family of solutions is a one-parameter family of circles x² + y² = C centred at the origin. Sweeping C traces out the whole family; every visible tangent in the slope field agrees with the active circle's tangent.

scenes.title: Newton's Law of Cooling: Exponential Approach
scenes.topic: Newton's law of cooling — the rate of temperature change is proportional to the gap from ambient: T'(t) = -k(T - T_a). Solve by separation to get T(t) = T_a + (T_0 - T_a)e^(-kt). Cooling curves from different starting temperatures all converge exponentially to the asymptote T_a — the universal 'rate proportional to gap' shape.

scenes.title: Characteristic Roots: Three Regimes of a 2nd-Order ODE
scenes.topic: Constant-coefficient 2nd-order linear ODE y'' + 2γy' + ω²y = 0. The ansatz y = e^(rt) gives the characteristic polynomial r² + 2γr + ω² = 0; its discriminant Δ = γ² − ω² classifies solutions into three regimes — overdamped, critically damped, underdamped. Sweep γ from 0 past ω and the solution morphs smoothly through all three.

scenes.title: Quadratic Taylor: A Plane Curves Into a Bowl
scenes.topic: Two-variable Taylor expansion to second order. The tangent plane (order 1) matches value + slopes; adding the Hessian quadratic form (order 2) matches curvature. A live order sweep k = 0 → 1 → 2 on a saddle slice shows the approximation snap into the true function and the residual |f − T_k| collapse.

scenes.title: Partial Derivatives: Slice the Surface, Read the Slope
scenes.topic: The geometric meaning of a partial derivative. Holding one variable fixed cuts the graph of f with a plane and leaves a one-variable curve; the partial is the slope of that curve at the point. As the slicing plane y = y₀ scrubs across the surface, the slice curve and the live slope readout update in sync — the partial is itself a function of position.

scenes.title: Clairaut's Theorem: Order Doesn't Matter
scenes.topic: Clairaut's (Schwarz's) theorem: for a smooth function f, the mixed partials commute — ∂²f/∂x∂y = ∂²f/∂y∂x. The two computation paths land on the same expression; geometrically, the corner-sum (f(x+h,y+k) − f(x,y+k) − f(x+h,y) + f(x,y))/(h·k) converges to the mixed partial regardless of slicing order as the rectangle shrinks. The Hessian is symmetric.

scenes.title: Gaussian Elimination: Two Lines, One Point
scenes.topic: Geometric meaning of Gaussian row reduction on a 2x2 system. The two lines tilt, slide, and become axis-aligned as row swaps and R2 ← R2 − 2·R1 are applied — but their intersection point, the unique solution (2, 1), stays pinned. Row operations change the picture of the lines without changing the truth they encode.

scenes.title: AB Means B First, Then A
scenes.topic: Matrix multiplication is function composition. Applying B then A to the unit square gives the same result as applying the single matrix AB. Swapping the order gives BA — a different parallelogram. Order is part of the operation: AB ≠ BA in general, and AB acts right-to-left (B first, then A).

scenes.title: Rotation Matrices Add Their Angles
scenes.topic: The rotation matrix R(θ) parametrises plane rotations. Sweeping θ from 0 to 2π rotates the basis around the unit circle with the matrix entries updating live to cos θ / sin θ. Composing R(30°) and R(45°) lands at R(75°): the matrix product equals R(α + β). Matrix multiplication, written as angle addition — geometry hiding inside arithmetic.

scenes.title: Cauchy–Schwarz: The Dot Product Has a Ceiling
scenes.topic: The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality caps the dot product by the product of lengths: |u·v| ≤ ‖u‖·‖v‖. Sweeping the angle traces u·v between the two horizontal ceilings ±‖u‖·‖v‖ and shows equality at θ = 0 and θ = π. This is the bound that lets cos θ live in [−1, 1].

scenes.title: QR: Gram–Schmidt as a Matrix Factorisation
scenes.topic: Gram–Schmidt packaged as a matrix factorisation A = QR. Normalise a₁ to q₁; subtract the projection of a₂ onto q₁ to get a perpendicular residual e₂; normalise e₂ to q₂. The lengths and projection coefficients pile up into an upper-triangular R; the orthonormal directions go into Q. A is rebuilt as Q times R.

scenes.title: Rotations Preserve the Dot Product
scenes.topic: An orthogonal matrix R satisfies RᵀR = I, so ⟨Ru, Rv⟩ = uᵀRᵀRv = ⟨u, v⟩. Sweep the rotation angle continuously and watch the live dot product stay constant while both vectors swing together — lengths, the angle between them, and the inner product all invariant. The algebraic chain (Ru)ᵀ(Rv) = uᵀIv = ⟨u,v⟩ closes the argument.

scenes.title: Gradient Descent: Walking Downhill
scenes.topic: Steepest descent finds a minimum by repeatedly stepping against the gradient, x_{k+1} = x_k − η∇f(x_k). On the anisotropic bowl f = ½(x² + 2.2y²) the iterate dives down the steep direction onto the valley floor, then crawls toward the minimum, and f decreases at every step. A value staircase tracks the monotone decrease.

scenes.title: Extrema on a Circle: Sweep the Boundary
scenes.topic: To optimise f = x² + 2y² on the unit circle, parametrise the boundary as (cos θ, sin θ); the two-variable constrained problem collapses to g(θ) = 1 + sin²θ. Its peaks at (0, ±1) are the constrained maxima, its troughs at (±1, 0) the minima, and at each extreme ∇f points along the radius — the Lagrange condition ∇f = λ∇g.

scenes.title: The Saddle Point: Up One Way, Down the Other
scenes.topic: At the origin of z = x² − y² the gradient vanishes but it is no extremum. Rotating a cutting plane through the centre morphs the cross-section z = r²·cos(2φ) from an upward parabola (a valley) through flat to a downward parabola (a ridge). Opposite curvature in the two principal directions means Hesse eigenvalues +2, −2 of opposite sign and discriminant D < 0 — the signature of a saddle.

scenes.title: Heun's Method: Predict, Then Correct
scenes.topic: Heun's method (improved Euler / explicit trapezoidal rule / Runge-Kutta order 2). Plain Euler reads only the start-of-step slope and drifts on a curving solution; Heun predicts the endpoint with an Euler step, samples the slope there, and steps with the average of the two slopes — one extra evaluation lifts the order from one to two.

scenes.title: Explicit vs Implicit: Why Backward Euler Stays Stable
scenes.topic: Forward (explicit) Euler reads the slope at the current point; backward (implicit) Euler reads it at the next point, so the unknown appears on both sides and must be solved. On y' = -λy, forward Euler multiplies by (1 - hλ) and blows up once h exceeds 2/λ, while backward Euler divides by (1 + hλ) and decays for any step — implicitness costs a solve per step but buys unconditional stability for stiff problems.

scenes.title: Numerical Orbits: Why Euler Spirals Off
scenes.topic: Integrating a system of ODEs in the phase plane. The oscillator x' = v, v' = -x has circular orbits of constant energy x^2 + v^2. Forward Euler steps along the tangent and multiplies the radius by sqrt(1 + h^2) > 1 each step, so the orbit spirals outward (energy injected); a fourth-order RK step at the same h stays on the circle. A method's geometry, not just its local accuracy, decides whether an invariant like energy is preserved.
